results.title: ANC NEC meets to put final stamp on mayoral candidates
results.description:
ANC NEC meets to put final stamp on mayoral candidates Nokuthula Khanyile Tue, 08/25/2026 - 09:28

JOHANNESBURG - The African National Congress is convening a special meeting in Johannesburg on Tuesday to finalise its mayoral candidates.

All indications are that the national executive committee meeting will approve the candidates before the end of this week.

The ANC says the party's leadership is expected to use this meeting to conclude the last phase of the candidate selection process for the November local government elections.

READ | Masina: No crisis as ANC delays mayoral candidate announcements

President Cyril Ramaphosa’s party is on the backfoot with its election programme.

It made a U-turn on Saturday after promising the nation to announce its mayoral candidates. The party chose to rather parade the top three candidates for every municipality.

results.title: Andy Burnham Refuses To Rule Out Raising Taxes In Autumn Budget
results.description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers closing remarks during the first National Day for victims and survivors of terrorism memorial event at Lancaster House in London, England, Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. Andy Burnham has insisted he “won’t be unrealistic” about the state of public finances and refused to rule out tax rises in the autumn Budget . The prime minister said Britons must understand the country is “in a challenging position” when asked how he would fund the public spending commitments he’s made during his first month in the job. Chancellor John Healey is expected to hike taxes when unveils the government’s spending plans on October 28, due to the economic fallout from the Iran war and the pressing need to increase defence spending. Speaking to ITV News , Burnham said: “I will always take a careful approach to things. I won’t take risks with people’s jobs or livelihoods or their family finances. “I will try to help them in whatever way I can and we have already done some things that will help them going forward. I will do what I can, but I won’t be unrealistic and people need to understand that. “We are in a challenging position. Whatever I do will be carefully thought through. It will be funded. That is exactly what I have done so far but there will be more to come as we go into the autumn.” The prime minister has promised to follow Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which vowed not to increase VAT, income tax or national insurance. Energy regulator Ofgem is expected to hike the energy price cap by 4% on Wednesday, up to £1,729 annually for the average household between October and December. Healey also needs to find at least £4.7 billion for extra defence spending along with funding for the cost of living promises Burnham has made since getting into office. The pressure from the Iran war has reportedly seen the government’s fiscal headroom decline from £22 billion to about £15 billion, while inflation also rose to 2.9% in July due to the conflict. Burnham also told ITV News he would not call an early election, saying: “An election just brings a load of point scoring, a load of arguments, a load of division. Actually what I’m going to try to do in this moment as prime minister is bring people together, get some hope going around the country.” Listen to Commons People, the podcast that makes politics easy. results.title: Trump veers from boredom to denial after 6 months of war on Iran
results.description: At an impromptu press conference last week, US President Donald Trump waxed lyrical about his helipad, his ballroom and his granite paving stones. The one thing he barely mentioned? The war on Iran Six months after launching what he expected to be a lightning offensive, Trump appears bored or even in denial about the conflict as it puts a drag on his second presidency. “Right now, the situation is so good,” Trump replied when asked about Iran, after leading reporters on a tour of the White House’s South Lawn to show off his latest renovations. During the 36-minute event, Trump used the word “granite” 13 times and the word “Iran” just three. But the war, in which at least 18 US service members have died and more than 750 were wounded, according to Pentagon figures, has become a millstone around Trump’s neck. Thousands more have died in Iran and Lebanon. US voters are angry about the war’s knock-on effect on the cost of living and crucial midterm elections are around the corner. Even his MAGA fans are questioning why the man who vowed to start no new foreign wars has got America into another quagmire with no apparent plan to get out of it. “Is there a rabbit in the hat? No, I think the hat is empty,” William Galston, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told AFP. ‘Very boring’ Trump’s public approval ratings have fallen since his return to office in 2025, and the drop accelerated after the United States and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted on August 14-17 found that his approval rating had fallen to 33 per cent, the lowest of his current term. Other major surveys also show Trump deep in negative territory. For Trump, Iran was meant to be a quick win like the US capture of Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro in January. In a telephone interview with AFP after the announcement of a ceasefire in April, Trump declared “total and complete victory”. But as the truce collapsed and Iran refused to bow to him, Trump has veered from military to economic pressure, just as his justifications for starting the war have changed from regime change to ensuring Iran doesn’t get a nuclear weapon. Then as Iran has kept its grip on the Strait of Hormuz — a pressure point that only came into play after Trump started the war — the 80-year-old has become first frustrated, and then disinterested. “Frankly, I thought they started to get very boring,” Trump said of the sputtering Iran talks as far back as June. Garret Martin, a foreign policy expert at American University, said Trump “famously has a short attention span”. “He was convinced that he could repeat a little bit what happened with Venezuela, a rapid show of force,” Martin told AFP. “I think now he’s in a position where there is no easy exit.” ‘Reckless war’ While Trump prefers to talk about the $400 million ballroom he is trying to build and puts his name on public buildings in Washington, voters are still thinking about Iran. “I think it’s completely unnecessary, and that it was a reckless war, and I think it’s going very badly,” said Joe Plenzler, a US Marine for 20 years. “The impact on the American consumer has gone up tremendously,” he said, adding that there was growing dissatisfaction in the rural, normally Republican area of Virginia where he lives. Gasoline prices have soared well above $4 per gallon since the start of the war, compared with the national average of $3.14 a year ago, with a huge knock-on effect on consumer prices. The reckoning for Trump could come in November’s midterm elections. Analysts say dissatisfaction with the war could cost the Republicans their control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate, scuppering Trump’s legislative plans and putting him at risk of a third impeachment. But has Trump completely checked out of the war? The 80-year-old’s search for a legacy after his second term ends in 2029 means it’s unlikely. “I think he cares about his standing in history,” said Galston. But he added: “Maybe he believes that statues and buildings and other things named for him will substitute for the kind of performance in office that makes you a memorable president”.
